items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: Half-life is a probability, not a clock
items.claim: A radioactive nucleus has a half-life of 5730 years. People imagine each atom has a 5730-year fuse. In fact each atom's decay is fundamentally random — no ageing, no internal clock.
items.prompt: If you watch a single carbon-14 nucleus for 5730 years, what is the chance it decays in the next year?

options.text: Almost 100 percent — it's used up its half-life
About 1 in 8267 — exactly the same as a freshly made C-14 nucleus

items.reveal:
The probability of decay per unit time (decay constant lambda) is fixed for a given isotope. A nucleus 'remembers' nothing about how long it has existed. For C-14, lambda equals ln 2 over 5730 years, so per year the decay chance is about 1 part in 8267 — for every individual nucleus, every year.

Half-life emerges from large populations of identical-but-independent random events. With one nucleus there is no half-life — only a probability distribution. With Avogadro's number of nuclei the law of large numbers makes the exponential decay law deterministic.

This is fundamentally different from human ageing or battery discharge — those have internal state that changes with time.
items.why: Half-life is intuitively pictured as countdown. It's actually a statistical property of populations of memoryless processes.

items.title: pH 1 is ten times more acidic than pH 2 — and a hundred times more than pH 3
items.claim: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 — looks linear. It's not. pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration. Each unit is a factor of ten.
items.prompt: How many times more H+ does stomach acid (pH 1) have than pure water (pH 7)?
items.reveal:
pH = -log10[H+]. Stomach acid at pH 1 has [H+] = 0.1 M. Pure water at pH 7 has [H+] = 10 to the minus 7 M. The ratio is 10 to the 6 — a million.

This is why diluting a strong acid even tenfold barely changes its pH — the absolute concentration drops by a factor of 10, but pH only shifts by 1 unit.

The same applies to the Richter scale (earthquakes), decibels (sound), and stellar magnitudes (brightness). Logarithmic scales let humans handle quantities spanning many orders of magnitude — but they hide the underlying spread.
items.why: Linear-looking scales can describe quantities ranging over 14 orders of magnitude. The arithmetic of acidity must respect the log.
